query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature sliding wear, FeNiCrCoCu coatings develop a dynamic ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer that promotes an inverse Hall‐Petch behavior, thereby reducing friction and wear.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating produced via conventional deposition methods with a standard (microcrystalline) grain structure.
generation.intervention: Expose the FeNiCrCoCu coatings to controlled high-temperature wear testing (e.g., 200–400 °C) under high contact loads designed to induce sustained shear stresses, and compare with room-temperature wear tests as a baseline.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear conditions (200–400 °C) under load where sustained sliding induces shear stress; oxidation should be minimal or controlled so that dynamic grain refinement is the dominant mechanism.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous near-surface layer (i.e., a highly refined microstructure in the deformed subsurface region).
generation.mechanism: The elevated temperature coupled with shear stress drives dynamic amorphization and grain refinement at the surface. This transformation leads to reduced effective shear strength via an inverse Hall‐Petch effect, enhancing grain-boundary sliding and local superplasticity, and thus lowering friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature wear conditions, the coating should exhibit a measurable transition to an ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous sublayer (detectable via TEM or EBSD) along with a reduced friction coefficient and lower wear rates compared to baseline (room-temperature) tests.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coatings tested under room-temperature conditions where such dynamic microstructural changes are minimal and wear behavior follows conventional mechanisms.
generation.boundary: This mechanism operates under high-temperature sliding conditions (approximately 200–400 °C) and under high loads typical for protective coatings; at temperatures well above this range or under different environmental conditions (e.g., aggressive oxidation), other degradation processes may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Due to compositional differences between FeNiCrCoCu and other studied HEAs (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi), the precise temperature/load thresholds for triggering the dynamic transformation and the degree of wear reduction are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings: one set subjected to high-temperature wear testing (200–400 °C under high load) and a baseline set tested at room temperature. Post-test, perform cross-sectional analysis (using TEM and EBSD) of the near-surface region to quantify grain size distribution and detect any formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous layer. Additionally, record friction coefficients and wear rates for both sets.
measurements: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) imaging of subsurface microstructure
Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) for grain size analysis
Wear volume or wear rate assessments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature tested samples do not exhibit a significant formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer relative to the baseline or if there is no statistically significant reduction in friction and wear rates under high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
